findings.summary: The caption opens with an administrative label instead of a hook, burying the actual hook in the second sentence.
findings.evidence: First sentence: "Part 2 of BINARY SEARCH PATTERNS." — the hook ("Binary search is not one problem, it is eight patterns wearing the same loop.") is only the second sentence.
findings.fix: Lead with the hook and move the part label later: "Binary search is not one problem, it is eight patterns wearing the same loop. Part 2 of BINARY SEARCH PATTERNS: seven handwritten pages take you from the overflow-safe mid formula to ..."

findings.summary: The complexity table states rotated-sorted-array search is O(log n) without qualification, but that bound only holds for distinct elements — with duplicates the worst case degrades to O(n).
findings.evidence: ["Rotated Sorted Array","O(log n)","O(1)"] and the pattern row ["Rotated (Find Target)","target in rotated","find sorted half, search inside it","index or -1"], alongside the pitfall bullet "Not handling ==duplicates== properly"
findings.fix: Change the row to "Rotated Sorted Array | O(log n) distinct, O(n) worst case with duplicates | O(1)", and note in the pattern row that when arr[low] == arr[mid] == arr[high] the sorted half is undecidable, so you must shrink low/high by one (LeetCode 81 behaviour).

findings.summary: The #java hashtag names a language that appears nowhere in the part's language-agnostic content.
findings.evidence: "#java" in hashtags, while the caption describes only "the overflow-safe mid formula to bounds, search-on-answer, rotated arrays, peaks, infinite arrays and 2D matrices" with no language mentioned.
findings.fix: Drop #java (or replace it with a content-relevant tag such as #problemsolving or #codingpatterns) unless the pages actually show Java code.

findings.summary: The Classic Binary Search key update omits the equality branch, so the rule as written can never return an index yet the Return column promises one.
findings.evidence: ["Classic BS","find target","arr[mid] < t: low = mid+1, else high = mid-1","index or -1"]
findings.fix: Write the update as "arr[mid] == t: return mid; arr[mid] < t: low = mid+1; else high = mid-1" so the two-way rule shown is actually the three-way comparison that produces the returned index.

findings.summary: Part 2 opens with an unlabeled tail of the page-7 "Common Mistakes" list whose first four items sit two slides earlier in Part 1, separated by the most-asked-questions list and the decision flowchart, so a learner reads the three red crossed items as a new, contextless list.
findings.evidence: Part 2 first block: {"type":"bullets","items":["Forgetting edge cases: empty array, single element","Not handling ==duplicates== properly","Missing boundary conditions in rotated arrays"],"style":"cross","frame":"dashed","ink":"red"} — the other four ("Wrong mid `(low + high) / 2` -> use `low + (high - low) / 2`", "Not updating low / high properly", "Wrong comparison operators (< vs <=)", "**Infinite loop** from wrong updates") are in parts/01/post.json on the "Mountain, Infinite Arrays & 2D Matrix Search" slide, before the "7. Interview Revision Sheet" heading.
findings.fix: Keep all seven mistakes in one list on the revision-sheet slide, or, if the split must stay for fill, prepend a labelling block to this first bullets block (e.g. {"type":"paragraph","text":"Common mistakes (continued)"}) so the three crossed items read as the tail of the earlier list rather than a new one.
